Kevin and Susan, certainly welcome to participate as much as you desire there so that as we go through, we won't be voting on any public hearing type of things tonight. Sure.

Hearing none. Chairman.

it's under there Chris's restoration plan and so we'll move on that when we get to your Sorry question on about that. If there are no other changes, we'll vote by unanimous consent. All in favor of those changes raise your hand or say aye. Aye.

Any opposed? And the motion to adjust the agenda passes five-zero-zero. Anybody with us tonight from the public to speak about something that's not on the agenda? Okay, at that point, we'll move on to old business. First up is going to be Bill Warner on the affordable housing plan. And Marina, if you can let me share the screen, I will try to get the presentation up.
All right. I think I have to make you a co host. And then I believe you should be able to share your screen now.
Okay there we go and at that point I'll turn it over to you Bill.

Very good. Thank you very much, and good evening, everyone. To summarize, I did this presentation a few weeks ago, and I've been working on the implementation section. And that's going very well. And really, the nuts and bolts of it, how to get things done and how we accomplish some of the things that we're going to talk about tonight. And I think I'll have a final draft to you by the end of March. So we're way ahead of schedule. They did amend the latest statute had affordable housing plans due to the state by June 30. So we're in very good shape. The first slide in front of you just summarizing what we've done in the past and what the last presentation talked about. And as you know, we talked about that there is sufficient affordable housing that is priced at a point that would be affordable to people making 80% immediate income,

but it doesn't meet the state definition because it is not deed restricted. So we saw a lot of housing that works for affordability, but not deed restricted. It doesn't meet the definition of state affordable housing. But as we'll talk about tonight, there's still a lot of people that are struggling that are maybe in those houses, but they're struggling to make their payments. So that is another need for affordable housing. These aren't necessarily homeless people. They're in their house and they're paying far more than 30% of their income to pay for housing costs. So that's a key issue. From the last meeting, we talked about the cost of construction, the land costs are going to make it very difficult to have to build affordable housing for any developer.

The lack of a down payment credit and student loan debt will also make it difficult for people looking to purchase houses is going to be difficult. There is no meaningful diversity in the housing stock in Andover. So it's pretty much all single family homes, a small handful of apartments in town. And new apartments could add diversity to the housing stock, both not only for young people that would like to stay in Andover, but also for empty nesters that would like to downsize and stay in town. And we we learned from the AARP that's in that I've a recent survey show that 80% of empty nesters and people wanting to downsize have a real desire to stay in the town that they've lived in. They do not wanna move to Florida or South Carolina. They don't wanna move to adjacent cities. They want to stay in the town that, they've spent their life in, and that that will be very difficult in Andover. So the next slide. So this what we're going talk about tonight is setting up what how many what is the goal what is the need for affordable housing and what should be our goal for this plan. I've reviewed probably 15 or 20 affordable housing plans now. And none of them really set a definite goal of we want to build this many houses. They talk about changing the regulations and hoping something will happen. I'd like to be more realistic about it and really start to say, Okay, this is what is reasonable that could be built, actually built in Andover to start addressing

some of that need. So to set the basis for that, we have to look at what's been going on. So population growth in the last ten years, the population in Andover has declined and it's projected to continue to decline out to 2,040. So we have a declining population in Andover. Next slide. We also have an aging population. Everybody understands the aging baby boomers. We've been talking about this for thirty years that we needed to plan for the aging population. The baby boom generation is getting older and older. So as you can see on this chart, I can't read it, but I think it's 1970. I think the median age was 28. That was when all of you were coming to Andover and building houses. The median age is half of the people are above that and half of the people are below that. So '28 was the median in 1970. You have now grown all the way up to twenty twenty to, I believe it says 44 or 48 is the median population. So half are above, half are below 48 now. That is very significant. 43% of your population in 2020 was 50 years old. So in ten years, probably half of your population with the aging population and younger people moving out, probably half of your population will be 60 years old. So you're going to have a lot of people that are probably starting to struggle being in a single family, in a large single family home on a large lot, which is the predominant housing type that you have in the town. So you're going to start to see that where people would like to downsize and don't have any options in Andover.

Next slide. Building permits. So so so as we talked about before, we have a declining population, we have an aging population. And now you look at building permits and this reflects exactly that. Since 2010, the great financial crisis, this is not unusual for every small town in Connecticut. The number of permits being issued for each year for new homes is down significantly. So from prior to 2010, you were building about 20 to 35 permits per year. When I was there working in Andover, the big one was the Haverhill subdivision on Long Hill Road. That's when they came in and they said, okay, we're going to divide the land and we're going to build houses. Completely on speculation, they didn't have contracts. And that's the way you did it before 2010. Everybody people would come build it and they'll come. After 2010, after the big financial crisis and all the banking reforms and everything else, it just became very, very difficult to do that. So from 2010 to the present, you've averaged about three to five permits per year. So going from 20 to 35 to three to five from 2010 to 2022. So that's a real significant decline in building permits. So you're not having a lot of houses aren't being built. So it's very hard for us to say we should build, you know, 10 affordable housing units a year when the market is only building three or three to five houses per year. Next slide. So as I talked about the speculative market was the Haverhill subdivision on Long Hill Road. The speculative market has not existed since the great financial crisis in twenty ten. So it's going to be very unlikely that Andover is going to meet the A-thirty

gs goal of 10% of your housing stock being affordable. So you need 82 more units to be of additional affordable units to meet that 10%. The statute requires that every project have 30% of the units as affordable. So what that boils down to is if every new development town had to be an affordable development with 30% of the units affordable, you'd have two seventy three new units with 191 of them being market rate and 82 of them being affordable. All you have to do is go back and look and see what the market is supporting for the last twelve years, three to five units a year. You're not going to get two seventy three housing units in a very, very long time.

Can I interrupt you for just a minute? Yeah. And then, so we've got 30% of a development needs to be affordable, you were saying. I think what we've really seen in Andover over the last bunch of years is one house at a time being built. Know, I don't know that we've, maybe this thing that you were just talking about, Haverhill, was the last subdivision that was even attempted.
Yeah, it probably was because that was right around 2010. And yeah, would be a
possibility we get no affordable housing because all we're doing is building one house here and there. Yeah, that's the speculative market. So the speculative market is

builders coming in buying land and putting in a subdivision with 10 houses and just knowing that people will show up and want houses. So they'll build houses, knowing that people are gonna come and buy them. That ended in 2010. And I would bet that 90% of the houses that were built in Andover since then, were people either downsizing and building a smaller house or people coming, selling their house somewhere else and building their dream house for themselves. It wasn't builders investing in building houses hoping somebody is going buy them. So it's just completely changed. You're right. So that's where we are with that. Okay, thank you.

So most likely will always be subject to a dash 30 gs. So there a long time prior to 2010, a dash 30 gs has been around for thirty years and the goal of small towns throughout Connecticut. And even if you read your your plans of development that I wrote in 2005 and 2015, we talked about how get out of the not be subject to eight dash 30 gs, achieve that 10% because it was realistic before the financial crash. But now it's probably not realistic. You're always going to be subject to eight thirty gs because understand, even if you have 9.5% of your houses as affordable, you're still subject to eight thirty gs. And if you get 10 houses built, that increases your 10% number. Let's make it easy. So if you had 100 houses built, your eight thirty gs number would go up because you had 100 more market rate. You'd have 10 more needed for affordable. So it's always something that you're probably not going to reach that goal. And again, it's the market really. So in other places, might read and I know Jed pointed one out in Marlborough or Colchester, where there is a strong market and somebody is building something with an affordable component under eight-thirty gs. And that's a question of the gap between the delta between the market rate units and the affordable units and what the prices are. So if you have a large if you have a very, very strong market, let's say in Fairfield County,

you can charge a lot more. You can get a premium on your market rate to cover the cost and the reduced rate for the affordable. So if there's a wide delta between them, you can do that. But in Andover and like most small towns in Central Connecticut, the difference between affordable and market is not that much. So you can't make it up in the market rate. And then the huge one that prevents any significant density and multifamily, which we learned when we did the incentive housing study, is the lack of public SOAR makes density very challenging. Next slide. So who should we target for new affordable housing and how many units should we create in the next ten years? Now, this is just my recommendation of how we should handle this. But what I think you need to do to get buy in for an affordable housing plan is really talk about the people of Andover. Not talking about solving the what people like to say, doing your fair share, the region's affordable housing issue and etcetera, etcetera, and affordable housing for people in the region. It's really comes down to in small towns is solving the affordable housing problem and helping the people of Andover.

So this what I'm writing, this is really focused on helping people that are in town that are struggling. And so what I'm doing is I look at it and say, who should the Supportable Housing Plan target? So we look at the Andover age distribution. And what I'm recommending is should be targeting young people that we hope want to stay in town and also baby boomers that are looking to downsize. The other ones are here or already established probably. The age demographic that I'm looking at in particular is ten to nineteen. And I say ten to nineteen because this is a ten year plan, you should be planning for the ten years. So ten to nineteen, these are going to be your buyers going to college coming back and buying houses are hoping to buy houses or looking for a place to live in their hometown.

And what that tells us is that there are four forty three people in that demographic, ten to nineteen year olds. And then under the fifty to sixty nine year olds, the baby boomers, the generation that would be looking to downsize in ten years. So it would be sixty to seventy nine in ten years. That population is a total of eleven seventy one people in your town. So these are people that are actually in your town that are looking to either stay in town when they come back from school or looking to downsize. So those are the people that we're targeting in this plan, if you all agree with my recommendation. So next slide. So some of those people may be perfectly fine and need any help in terms of affordable housing or downsizing. They may be affluent, they may have places to live, they may be okay. But we know in Andover that that 18% of your population is paying either mortgage or rent in excess of 30% every month for housing.

So that is when the housing crisis starts when they're paying more than 30% of their income for housing. So we know 18% of people are paying between 3050% of their income for housing costs. Okay. And then we know another 4% are paying over 50% for housing. So that's really staggering. So if they're making percent of your income in a month goes to paying either your rent or your mortgage taxes and utilities. So those are the people that are struggling with affordable housing. They may have housing, they may be in those houses that we identified as affordable sales, but they're having a real tough time paying the rent. So then this goes into some numbers of how we figure out that. And I take those numbers. And I think those numbers are probably fairly consistent, and they probably will stay true as we move as we as we go through through time. So we took that 10 19 year old age population.

So four forty three people between 10 and 19 years old, we apply 4% of that is 18 residents and 18% of that is 80 residents. That's the number of people that would need help with affordable housing. And then same for the baby boom generation, where we take the eleven seventy one. Now, probably the majority of them are two person households. So we divide that number by two to come up with households. So that's four fifty households between fifty and sixty nine that need affordable housing. And that comes down to 18 households at four percent and eighty one households at 18%.

Another question on this slide is, you had 18% that spend between thirty and fifty, and 4% spending more than 50, wouldn't be the high end of the need for housing be 22% as opposed to just 18%? It looks like all of those folks need helpers, that 4% included in the 18?

The four is in the 18. Yeah, it probably would have been easier to put them together, but I just wanted to show create a high and a low. Yep, okay. So the severe, the high, we know I guess it's just the opposite. The real need, the severe need is the 4%. And that means we have a need of 36 units. So there's 4% of your population that's paying over 50% for housing costs. And that comes out to 36 units. And then on the high end, where they're paying between 3050%, that's 160 units. Okay, so next slide. So it's interesting to look back at eight dash 30 gs and it's easy to say, well, eight dash 30 gs is unrealistic, we will never build that many, but it's pretty accurate in terms of what is needed. So eight dash 30 gs says the Andover needs 133 affordable units. And the math that we just did prior to that says we need 196 units because based on need, based on people that actually needed are paying a lot for housing. So HS30G in that sense is pretty accurate. And we know that HS 30 gs we only have 51 affordable units in town now. So you'd need another 82 to meet that goal. Next slide. Hey, Bill, can I ask a question? Yep.

So you're talking about the the targeted market. We're talking about the the very young and and the older crowd, but aren't there subsets of the other age brackets where we would need to address as well? Or are we assuming they don't need affordable housing?

Yeah, there certainly are, I'm sure. What we're trying to do is say, okay, for the next ten years, how many do we need and who are we really targeting on this? So, you know, and I think really what's going to happen is is it's going to be the empty nesters for sure, because that's going to be the majority of the town. And then the younger people that we would like to keep in town. I think the goal of the plan, you say, okay, well, who is the population that we're going to focus on? And the focus is going to be on those two groups. Yes, in the middle, probably you have a lot of people in the middle that have two incomes that are doing much, much better. So I think the two focus groups are the ones that are the most sensitive, but certainly there are people in the middle that are struggling too.
Okay, thanks.

This slide is just a it's just a timeline just just to show that if we take our numbers and we say between thirty six and one hundred and sixty units, 36 units per year is four per year. And 160 units is nine sixteen per year. And then we think back to what we talked about how many houses are getting built in town. Does this make any sense? Does it can it can it happen? Can we really make a recommendation that, you know, this is how many we need and this is what we're what our goal is. And it really doesn't. The next slide I say let's be realistic. And I think that's that's what a plan should be a plan should be realistic you can come up with all these which unfortunately a lot of planets do, they come up with all these pie in the sky ideas about building all this affordable housing and we need to do this and it's all these reasons why it's so good, but they're not realistic. They're not based in the market and the market is going to dictate how many get built because it's not going to be the government building them. It's going to be the market and hopefully when we come up with our recommendations, how we can attract developers and people in the market to create more affordable units. So again, if you look at on left

market rate units, those the actual numbers from 2,009 all the way up to August of last year. So there there just aren't 36 four four units per year or between four and sixteen units per year of affordable. So that is actual market rate units that are being built. So 2009 to 2021, you had 49 single family homes built. So rounding up to 50 units in ten years. So roughly 50 units in ten years was built by the private sector. That's an average of five homes per year. And we're looking at this and I'd say, okay, so how many of those five homes should we realistically say we want to target? How many affordable units should we

create? So A-thirty gs says 10% of all new units in in the town should be affordable. So that's that's one of the goals of a dash 30 gs. So that equals a half a dwelling affordable dwelling unit per year. And then if and 30% in a development, a dash 30 says 30% of all the units in a development should be affordable, so that would come out to 1.5 affordable units per year. So that's about as realistic as you could get. I mean, I can't picture the market completely turning around and young home home buyers flocking to Andover. I don't think we're going to see a lot of change. The state doesn't project a lot of change. The population is projected to continue to decline and continue to age. So I think what we're looking at is a realistic, a small town in Eastern Connecticut, making a realistic approach and a realistic goal to providing some affordable housing in their town, which I think is about all that really can be expected of a town in the Andover situation of Andover size. So what we have is the next slide. Andover's affordable housing goal. So the goal is to create between five and fifteen affordable units in the next ten years, targeted to Andover's empty nesters interested in downsizing and Andover's ten to nineteen year old age cohort also known as generation Z.

So in the next ten years, five to 15 affordable units. So if you think about that and you say, well, that's nothing. Well, that is a lot based on the current market and the fact that there have been no affordable units created in probably the last thirty years in Andover. So it's a way to start making a difference in the town. So the next next meeting, what we'll start to do is talk about how to do this. What kind of strategies could the town adopt to start taking this seriously and making a change? And, you know, lots of towns, and I'm sure this is exactly what's going to happen. Lots of towns are going to achieve their goal of affordable housing plan by June 30 and put it on the shelf and be done and wait. And and then in five years, was, oh, we gotta update this and they'll come up with some kind of update and that and that's all that will happen.

I think in Andover and in small town like this, you have the ability if there's the energy to do this and the need is identified to say, hey, let's let's let's do this. So the recommendations I'm going to make be making are are implementable and things that could really create an interest in doing it and a way to do it to start creating an affordable unit maybe every year or two or three units every year, depending on how aggressive you want to get. At the end, we'll also have an aggressive option, which gives you an idea of how to really go about it and aggressively go after something. So that's what that's what's going to come. And like I said, I think end of March, I should have a draft report and be ready for your next meeting to present the how to, what's next, where to, where and how do we get this done. And I'm open to any questions.

Bill, what comes after, you know, we get the plan, let's say, you know, March 21, the next meeting. And then at some point, I know before we submit the plan, we want to hold a public hearing. And I'm trying to figure out where does the public hearing and what are the other big wickets, you know, was there a brief to the Board of Selectmen or Board of Finance? I couldn't remember, but what are the big chunks that we as a commission have to hop through before we can deliver the goods and say we're done?

Yeah, I mean, think I know it's a tough time with the budget and everything else, but I really think it's critical because the recommend planning and zoning can only do so much. The recommendations that I'm making are going to involve Board of Finance and Board of Selectmen as well. It's because it's a financial thing. It's a tax thing. It's it's favorable tax assistance, grants, etc. So it's going to involve all three boards, Board of Finance, Board of Selectmen and Planning and Zoning. So I think before you really initially, know, kick it off with the public, that's discussion, a discussion or something, introducing it to the Board of Finance and the Board of Selectmen is critical. And then public workshop or public hearing, probably a workshop without the formality of a public hearing because you don't have to have a public hearing on this. But you can advertise and everything, but maybe be more informal with a public workshop to explain what needs to be done. And then from there, go forward with probably ideally, PNC would approve it and Board of Selectmen would approve it, and then you'd send it off to the state for telling them here's our affordable housing plan.
Okay. Any any of the other commission members have any questions of Bill while we're on this topic?

Yeah, Bill, once again really nice job, very comprehensive presentation and you know well organized easy to follow. Question I have is if we put together an affordable housing plan and it doesn't get us to close the gap from where we are now, and, you know, are there consequences with the state if we don't have a plan that gets us to, you know, be in compliance with eight dash 30 g?

No. There are not. No. So the only thing is you're subject to eight thirty eight dash 30 which I, in my opinion, all of you are always going to be no matter what your plan says, because you're just not going to build that many houses. So there is, there are no penalties. Even if you, even if you didn't do this plan, you said, I would, we can't be bothered. The only penalty is that if you apply for a grant, you have to include a letter saying that you did not, you are not in compliance with requirement to have an affordable housing plan. That's the only teeth that this has.
Okay, thank you. So as long as we have a plan, we're in compliance, and then it's just a matter of how, you know, whether we're addressing the need.

Exactly, and that really comes down to the town. And like I said, I, there's, there's a lot of opportunities right now with COVID money and grants and there's, there's a lot of money there and there is a way to put together funds that can create affordable housing rehab programs. I'm starting to go into all the stuff that I'm going to talk about next month, but you know, a lot of different programs that could help people because you know, you may have an affordable, you could say you're going to give a, for instance, I'll just give a quick one. For instance, let's say you have a couple that's in a house that is having trouble getting upstairs. I think my own parents, they couldn't use the stairs anymore. So they had to create a bathroom downstairs, a full bath downstairs, move the bedroom downstairs, move the washer and dryer from the basement upstairs. And they had to do all that. Fortunately, they had the ability to do that, but there are some people that may not have the ability to do that. So you could create, and this would be completely eligible for low to moderate income, a grant program, tax be even type program that would all help them to do those things in exchange for putting in a restriction on that unit and then you would be creating an affordable unit.
Very good. Thanks.

Sure. Anybody else? I did have a couple more questions comments for you, Bill. And what actually does it mean when we say that a property is going to be deed restricted? What does that mean to the person who owns that property?

What it means is that the unit can only be increased, can only increase the appreciation in the value of the house, can only increase by the consumer price index. So right now that would be very unfavorable. Past ten years, it'd be, wouldn't be too bad. But, but right now, because we have the consumer price index at 8% housing costs going up like crazy, that would be the concern.

And for the Commission, I did attend Marlborough's. They had a working session. I thought it was a public hearing, but it was only, you know, what Bill referred to as the information session. I thought that was pretty good. It was pretty basic, you know, the stuff that we talked about in the last two sessions. But there were a couple of things that I took away from that, maybe just because it's the same information was presented a little bit differently. And Steve, when you asked the question about aren't there people in need through all these different age groups, I think the thing, you know, this presentation showed median incomes for the different age groups. And one of the things that I took away, and it shows that Bill's targeting the right groups, is that, you know, the median income for the retirees, you know, is significantly less than the Andover median income, which is like $100,000 a year. You know, the average for a retiree is 50,000 or $60,000 So, you know, all the retirees are down below the 60% threshold on that. And you can envision a similar thing with the young folks just starting out. So, not only do we have big age groups there to target and keep in Andover, but those are certainly the ones that are struggling the most with buying. I guess another thing that I took away, and Bill showed us a bunch of pictures that, you know, what is affordable housing? You know, it was nice looking stuff. This is nothing that you wouldn't want to live in. And I think the way it was described at this other presentation was if a guy makes a subdivision in the market price houses are all 1,800, 2,000 square foot,

the only difference in the quality between that and the affordable is most likely in the size of the house. So to get the house down in size, they would just reduce the square footage. And they might not put a garage on it, you know, leaving the ability to put that on afterwards. And that's how, you know, the developers are getting down there. Maybe this is all stuff that Bill was going to talk about next month, not sure. And then the third thing that was kind of funny is there was a guy from the Board of Finance at the presentation. And, you know, Marlboro, just like us, talked about the increasing age population

and they discussed the number of kids in the school going down. And this guy said, you know, I just went to the Board of Education meeting last week and they showed how the school age population was projected to increase over the next ten years. And didn't really have an answer to it. The answer that was provided was well, they're not right. These are the right numbers. You know, these are provided by the state. But it was, I'm sure I read the story in the River East a week or so ago and it talked about, you our population was no longer declining at the school, but in fact was going up a little bit. So, it's pretty similar to what we had. And at the same time, they were looking at, you know, wrapping up in June, having public hearing in June to submit the plan. So, we're pretty consistent with what I saw over there. But that was a very informal session that allowed people to ask questions. Well, I guess the other thing that was a lot of discussion at that meeting was how do we incentivize people that have the naturally occurring affordable housing to put a deed restriction on their house? Now, were indicating that you could only go up 7.5% over what you bought it for. And they didn't really explain that maybe that was on a yearly thing based on the consumer price index. So that discussion thinking that if you owned a house for twenty years, can only sell it for 7.5% more than you bought it for. And that certainly didn't get anybody excited.
Yeah, no, 7.5% would be this year. Yeah, this year. Yeah, it's an annual.

I think, you know, I'll work with you offline to try and figure out how do we build the presentation for both the public and the Board of Select and Board of Finance get that and And so when June comes here, we can declare victory. Sounds great.
